item.research_question: How do cold rolling and subsequent annealing treatments at different temperatures (800, 900, and 1000 °C) affect the microstructural evolution, specifically the formation of B2 precipitates and recrystallization states, and how do these microstructures influence the tensile strength and ductility of Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys?
item.processing_route: Melted via magnetic levitation induction at 1600 °C, homogenized at 1150 °C for 24 h, cold-rolled to ~70% thickness reduction, and annealed at 800, 900, or 1000 °C for 60 min followed by water cooling.
item.test_conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests performed at room temperature with a strain rate of 10−3/s; hardness measured with 200 g load and 15 s dwell time.
key_findings: The 800 °C-annealed specimen exhibited a partially recrystallized microstructure with quasi ultra-fine grains (~0.9 ± 0.6 μm) and a yield strength of ~870 ± 1.6 MPa.
The 900 °C-annealed specimen showed full recrystallization with fine grains (~2.2 ± 1.6 μm) and a B2 precipitate volume fraction of ~2.2 ± 0.3%.
The 1000 °C-annealed specimen displayed grain coarsening (~7.2 ± 5.3 μm) and a reduced B2 precipitate volume fraction of ~0.6 ± 0.1%.
B2 precipitates along grain boundaries increased in size from ~198 ± 84 nm (800 °C) to ~263 ± 146 nm (1000 °C) while their volume fraction decreased.
Small, elongated B2 precipitates were aligned along deformation twins in the non-recrystallized region of the 800 °C-annealed specimen.
The 800 °C-annealed specimen maintained a high ductility of ~25.5 ± 2.4% despite the high strength.
Precipitation strengthening contributed only ~10.5% and ~9.1% to the yield strength in 900 °C- and 1000 °C-annealed specimens, respectively.
Grain boundary strengthening was identified as the main mechanism for strength enhancement in fully recrystallized specimens.
item.mechanism: The superior strength in the 800 °C-annealed specimen is attributed to heterogeneous microstructures combining quasi ultra-fine recrystallized grains, non-recrystallized grains with high dislocation density and deformation twins, and B2 precipitates, which also generate significant back-stress during deformation. In fully recrystallized states, strength is primarily driven by grain boundary strengthening (Hall-Petch effect), while precipitation strengthening plays a weak or neglected role due to the semi-coherent nature and size of the B2 precipitates.
item.limitations: The study notes that more detailed investigations are needed to determine the critical conditions for recrystallization onset/completion and B2 precipitation/dissolution quantitatively, and that the contribution of precipitation strengthening is associated with specific precipitate parameters that require further optimization.
item.future_work: More studies about the kinetics of B2 precipitation and dissolution should be conducted to understand the variation trend of the size and volume fraction with increasing the annealing temperature, and detailed investigations should be done to determine the critical conditions for recrystallization and B2 phase transitions.
quotes: The yield strength and ultimate tensile strength in 800 °C-annealed specimen were raised as high as ~870 and ~1060 MPa and the ductility was maintained at ~26%.

The strengthening behavior derived from the heterogeneous microstructures consisting of quasi ultra-fine recrystallized grains, non-recrystallized grains, deformation twins, dislocations, and B2 precipitates.
The B2 phases tend to precipitate along the grain boundaries in the recrystallized region and along the deformation twins in the non-recrystallized region.
